## FULL FEATURE INVENTORY (must all be rebuilt)

### 1. Authentication & Roles
- Two auth surfaces: **Admin** (`role='admin'`) and **Driver** (`role='driver'`), both backed by Supabase Auth against the same `auth.users`/`profiles` table.
- Admin login + forgot-password/reset-password flow.
- Driver login, signup (via invite-only flow), forgot-password/reset-password flow.
- A neutral `/login` redirect route that sends the user to the correct portal based on role.
- **Driver invites**: admins create an invite (`driver_invites` table: email, full_name, location); driver signup page validates the invite exists/unused, creates the auth user, and the DB trigger auto-creates a `profiles` row (`driver_id` like `DRV-XXXXXX`, default role `driver`).
- Row Level Security throughout: drivers can only see their own resources; admins (checked via a `public.is_admin()` SQL function) can see/manage everything.

### 2. Regions (Cape Town / Joburg)
- A region toggle in the admin shell, persisted to `localStorage`.
- All admin data views (fleet, drivers, bookings, fines, etc.) filter by the selected region.
- `profiles`, `vehicles`, `bookings` each have a `location` column (`'Cape Town' | 'Joburg'`, default `'Cape Town'`); `driver_invites.location` has no default (set at invite time).
- Region pre-checks run before vehicle/driver availability checks so cross-region assignment is impossible.

### 3. Admin Dashboard / Booking Calendar
- Month-grid calendar of bookings, color-coded by vehicle, with paid (green) / unpaid (orange) indicator classes driven by `receipt_number` presence.
- Booking CRUD modal: client name, route, tour reference, start/end date+time, assigned driver, assigned vehicle (owned **or** rented), status (`pending|confirmed|invoiced|completed|cancelled`), payment status, receipt number, notes.
- Booking documents: multi-file upload (Cloudinary), thumbnailed list (images get thumbnails, PDFs/Word get icons, shows size + upload date), collapses to a `<details>` element at 5+ files.
- Itinerary upload: separate single-file slot from general documents; driver sees a "View Itinerary" button on their task card only when set.
- Booking completion lock: completed bookings become read-only except via the edit-approval flow.
- **Booking edit/delete approval workflow**: editing or deleting a confirmed/locked booking requires either an OTP (if enabled) or admin confirmation; every change writes a `booking_edit_log` row (action `edit`/`delete`, reason, old/new JSONB snapshots). Delete requests go through `booking_delete_requests` (reason + `cancellation_type`: `mistake` or `client_cancelled`) and show in a "Pending Deletions" admin view with Approve/Reject.
- Active trips / upcoming trips views, and a bookings archive.
- "Download booking package" — bundles documents/itinerary/PDF for a booking.

### 4. Fleet (Vehicles) Management
- CRUD for vehicles: registration no. (unique), make, model, year, current mileage, next-service-km, status (`active|maintenance|decommissioned`), color (hex, used for calendar bars), notes, region.
- Fleet table view with status + location filter dropdowns.
- Maintenance alerting: an Edge Function checks bookings ending within 2 days and emails an alert (`maintenance_alert_sent` flag prevents duplicates); admin can manually re-trigger per booking.

### 5. Rented-In Vehicles
- Separate `rented_vehicles` table (supplier, reg no, make, model, dates, daily rate, supplier ref, status, notes) for vehicles hired from third parties to cover overflow.
- Rented vehicles can be assigned to a booking and to a driver; bookings store `is_rented_vehicle`, `rented_vehicle_id`, `rented_vehicle_reg`, `rented_vehicle_model`.
- Drivers can see rented vehicles only when assigned to them; admins see/manage all.
- Dedicated admin page with stats, add/edit modal, and "assign to booking" flow.

### 6. Drivers Management
- Admin "Manage Drivers" table (name, driver ID, phone, status, location, etc.) with edit/deactivate/delete and location+status filters.
- Driver invite flow (see Auth section).

### 7. Vehicle Inspections (Pre-trip / Post-trip)
- Driver-facing inspection form tied to a booking + vehicle: configurable checklist (JSONB), pass/fail/flag per item, free-text notes, current mileage, photo/video capture per item (Cloudinary), and a derived `has_critical_fault` flag.
- Submitting a critical fault triggers a `fault-alert` Edge Function (email/WhatsApp-style alert) and sets `alert_sent`.
- Admin inspections list/detail view; PDF export of a completed inspection checklist (with embedded signature — see PDF section).
- Inspections also support rented vehicles (`is_rented_vehicle`, `rented_vehicle_model`), and rented-vehicle registrations are **not** constrained by the FK to the owned fleet table.

### 8. Weekly Recon Sheets (driver trip cost & wellness report)
- One sheet per driver per week (`week_start`/`week_end`): tour reference/vehicle, vehicle reg, start/end KM, total distance, trips completed, total hours, cost line items (free text), trip budget/cost, driver food, flights to/from, driver rate, accommodation, total profit/loss, director sign-off.
- Wellness/condition fields: vehicle issues, accidents/incidents, traffic violations, safety concerns, maintenance needed, fuel consumption, tyre condition, fatigue level (1–10), stress level (1–10), health issues, free-text driver notes.
- Slip/receipt image uploads (`slip_image_urls` JSONB array).
- Status lifecycle: `draft → submitted → reviewed`, with `reviewed_by`/`reviewed_at`.
- **Edit-request workflow after submission**: driver requests an edit (`edit_request_status: pending`, with a reason); admin approves (requires OTP if `OTP_ENABLED`, otherwise a confirm dialog) or rejects (with rejection reason). Driver sees their edit-request status as a badge in their recon history.
- Admin "Recon Review" list + detail view; PDF export (`downloadReconPDF`).

### 9. Transfer Recon Sheets (weekly transfer-payment form)
- Separate from the trip recon sheet: one row per transfer completed that week, stored as a `transfers` JSONB array (add/remove rows in the UI).
- Same `draft → submitted → reviewed` lifecycle and the same edit-request → admin approve/reject (OTP-gated) pattern as weekly recon sheets, fully independent state.
- Admin "Transfer Recon Review" list + PDF export (`downloadTransferReconPDF`).

### 10. Wages Reconciliation
- Admin view combining recon sheets + transfer recon sheets for payroll reconciliation across a period/region.

### 11. Vehicle Expenses & Damages
- Drivers (or admin directly) log: expense type (`Tyres|Service|Damage|Repair|Accident|Other`), description, amount, expense date, supporting documents + photos (Cloudinary, JSONB arrays with filename/size/resource_type/uploaded_at).
- Approval lifecycle: `pending → approved/rejected` with `reviewed_by`, `reviewed_at`, `rejection_reason`.
- Notification on submission via `notify-expense-submitted` Edge Function; `alert_sent`/`driver_notified_at` tracked.
- Drivers see only their own expense records; admins see/manage all, by vehicle/driver/status/date.

### 12. Traffic Fines
- Admin logs a fine against a booking + vehicle + driver: fine timestamp, reference, location, description, amount, notification email (validated format).
- "Lookup driver by fine time" helper — given a vehicle + timestamp, finds which driver/booking was active at that moment.
- Notifies the driver via `notify-driver-fine` Edge Function; tracks `email_sent`/`email_sent_at`/`notification_error`.
- Admin Traffic Fines dashboard (filterable by vehicle/driver/region); drivers see their own fines history.

### 13. Incident Reports
- Driver-submitted: incident type, description, location, injuries flag, photos + documents (Cloudinary), linked to a booking where applicable.
- Lifecycle: `reported → reviewed → closed`, with admin notes, `reviewed_by`/`reviewed_at`.
- Admin Incident Reports list/detail with notes + status change; driver-side incident history tab.

### 14. Vehicle Checklists
- A distinct (separate from inspections) periodic vehicle condition checklist drivers submit, joined to `profiles` for driver name display.
- Admin list/detail view + PDF export (`downloadChecklistPDF`); driver-side "My Checklists" tab.

### 15. Documents
- Driver "My Documents" tab aggregating all files the driver has uploaded/received across bookings (itinerary, booking documents) for quick access.

### 16. OTP Security Layer (feature-flagged)
- `otp_verifications` table: hashed OTP, resource type (`recon_edit|booking_edit|booking_delete|expense_approval`), resource id, 15-minute expiry, attempt counter.
- Two Edge Functions: `send-otp-email` (emails a one-time code to the admin) and `verify-otp` (validates hash + expiry + attempt limit).
- Gated by a single config flag (`OTP_ENABLED`, default `false`). When `false`, the same approval actions fall back to a plain confirmation dialog — the **same business logic path** must run either way (single source-of-truth "perform the approved action" function, only the gate before it differs).
- Used for: recon edit approval, transfer recon edit approval, booking edit, booking delete approval, expense approval.

### 17. Cloudinary Upload Architecture (replicate exactly)
- All uploads go through a Supabase Edge Function `sign-upload` that returns `{ signature, timestamp, api_key, cloud_name, upload_preset, folder, type: 'upload' }`.
- The browser uploads directly to Cloudinary's API using those signed params — `type: 'upload'` is forced even if the underlying preset is "authenticated", so the resulting `secure_url` is always a plain public URL (no signed delivery URL needed, no expiry).
- A `get-signed-url` Edge Function exists for any case still needing a signed delivery URL.
- Write a `getDocumentUrl(doc)` utility that normalizes a document/photo record into a URL string and gracefully handles legacy malformed records (objects that look like `{"0":"h","1":"t",...}` — a stringified URL that got spread into an object). **Every** place that renders a document/photo URL must go through this helper — never read `.url` directly.

### 18. PDF Generation
- Client-side PDF generation (port the `pdf-lib`-based approach) for: inspection checklists (with embedded driver signature — base64 → stripped data-URI → `Uint8Array`, scaled to fit, with a bordered "Signature on file [timestamp]" fallback when no image is available), weekly recon sheets, transfer recon sheets, vehicle checklists, and a combined "booking package" download.

### 19. Desktop / Responsive Layout
- Mobile-first sidebar nav that becomes a permanently-visible left sidebar at ≥1025px (no overlay/close button at that breakpoint); main content gets a left margin and wider padding on desktop.

### 20. PWA
- Installable manifest (name `INYATHI`, icons), offline app-shell caching via a service worker, registered once on the client.

## DATABASE SCHEMA (port these tables/columns/constraints faithfully)

Recreate, with RLS enabled and policies matching the access rules in each feature section above:

- `profiles` (extends `auth.users`: driver_id, name, phone, email, role, is_active, location, timestamps) + `handle_new_user()` trigger that auto-creates a profile (`driver_id = 'DRV-' || upper(substring(uuid,1,6))`) on signup.
- `vehicles` (registration_no unique, model, make, year, current_mileage, next_service_km, status, color, location, notes, timestamps).
- `bookings` (invoice_no unique, client_name, route, tour_reference, start/end date+time, rental_period tstzrange, assigned_driver_id → profiles.driver_id, assigned_vehicle_reg → vehicles.registration_no, status, payment_status, receipt_number unique-partial-index, booking_documents JSONB, itinerary_url/filename/uploaded_at, maintenance_alert_sent(+at), last_modified_at, modification_reason, is_rented_vehicle, rented_vehicle_id/reg/model, location, notes, timestamps).
- `inspections` (invoice_no → bookings.invoice_no, vehicle_reg → vehicles.registration_no [FK dropped to support rented regs], driver_id → profiles.driver_id, inspection_type pre-trip/post-trip, checklist_json, faults_json, media_urls, pdf_urls, mileage_at_inspection, notes, has_critical_fault, alert_sent, is_rented_vehicle, rented_vehicle_model, created_at).
- `recon_sheets` (driver_id, week_start/end, tour_reference/vehicle, vehicle_reg, start/end_km, total_distance_km, trips_completed, total_hours, cost_lines_text, trip_budget/cost, driver_food, flights_to/from, driver_rate, accommodation, total_profit_loss, director_sign_off, wellness fields (vehicle_issues, accidents_incidents, traffic_violations, safety_concerns, maintenance_needed, fuel_consumption, tires_condition, fatigue_level 1-10, stress_level 1-10, health_issues, driver_notes), slip_image_urls, admin_review_notes, edit_request_* fields, status draft/submitted/reviewed, submitted_at, reviewed_by/at, timestamps).
- `transfer_recon_sheets` (driver_id, week_start/end, transfers JSONB, status, edit_request_* fields, submitted_at, reviewed_by/at, timestamps).
- `driver_invites` (email PK, full_name, location, invited_by, invited_at, used_at).
- `otp_verifications` (admin_id, resource_type [recon_edit|booking_edit|booking_delete|expense_approval], resource_id, otp_hash, created_at, expires_at default +15min, verified_at, attempts).
- `booking_edit_log` (booking_id, admin_id, action [edit|delete], reason, old_values/new_values JSONB, approved_at, created_at).
- `booking_delete_requests` (booking_id, requested_by, reason, cancellation_type [mistake|client_cancelled], status [pending|approved|rejected], rejection_reason, reviewed_by/at, created_at).
- `vehicle_expenses` (vehicle_reg, driver_id [nullable], logged_by_admin_id [nullable], expense_type [Tyres|Service|Damage|Repair|Accident|Other], description, amount, expense_date, document_urls/photo_urls JSONB, status [pending|approved|rejected], submitted_at, reviewed_by/at, rejection_reason, alert_sent, driver_notified_at, timestamps).
- `rented_vehicles` (supplier, reg_no, make, model, start/end_date, daily_rate, supplier_ref, status, notes, assigned_booking_id, assigned_driver_id, created_at).
- `traffic_fines` (booking_id, vehicle_reg, driver_id, fine_timestamp, fine_reference, location, description, amount, notification_email [format-checked], email_sent(+at), notification_error, logged_by_admin_id, timestamps).
- `incident_reports` (booking_id, driver_id, vehicle_reg, incident_type, description, location, injuries, photo_urls/document_urls JSONB, status [reported|reviewed|closed], admin_notes, reviewed_by/at, timestamps).
- `vehicle_checklists` (driver_id → profiles.driver_id FK for joins, plus whatever checklist/condition fields fit the "vehicle checklist" feature described above — infer a reasonable JSONB-based structure consistent with the other checklist-style tables since the exact columns weren't in the exported schema file; document this assumption in `MIGRATION_NOTES.md`).

Include: `is_admin()` SECURITY DEFINER helper to avoid recursive RLS; `set_updated_at()` trigger function reused across tables; appropriate indexes (driver/vehicle/date/status lookups) mirroring the original.

## EDGE FUNCTIONS (port 1:1, Deno + Resend API, in `supabase/functions/`)

`sign-upload`, `get-signed-url`, `driver-invite`, `fault-alert`, `check-vehicle-maintenance`, `notify-driver-fine`, `notify-expense-submitted`, `send-otp-email`, `verify-otp`. Keep their request/response contracts identical so the frontend rewrite is a drop-in swap. `check-vehicle-maintenance` should remain triggerable both manually (POST `{booking_id}`) and on a nightly `pg_cron` schedule.

## NON-FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS

- Strong client-side form validation mirroring the DB `CHECK` constraints (status enums, fatigue/stress 1–10, email format, amounts ≥ 0).
- Loading/empty/error states on every data view.
- Toast/inline error surfacing for Supabase/Edge Function failures (mirror `getFunctionErrorMessage`-style human-readable error mapping).
- Keep all RLS-driven access control as the actual security boundary — UI-side role checks are convenience only, never the only guard.
- A `README.md` covering: env var setup, Supabase project setup (schema + migrations + edge function deploy + secrets), Cloudinary setup, `next build` static export, and deploy steps for both Vercel and Netlify.

## DELIVERY PLAN — build in this order

1. Scaffold Next.js project (static export config), Tailwind (or the equivalent of the original `style.css` design tokens), base layout, env handling, Supabase client singleton, and typed DB schema.
2. Port `supabase/schema.sql`, all migrations, and all Edge Functions unchanged into the new repo's `supabase/` folder.
3. Build auth: admin + driver login/signup/forgot/reset, route guards, role-based redirect.
4. Build the admin shell (sidebar, region toggle, desktop breakpoint) and driver shell (tabs).
5. Build each feature module from the inventory above, one at a time, in this order: Fleet → Drivers/Invites → Bookings/Calendar → Inspections → Recon Sheets → Transfer Recon → OTP layer → Vehicle Expenses → Rented Vehicles → Traffic Fines → Incident Reports → Vehicle Checklists → Wages Reconciliation → Reports/Archive → Pending Deletions.
6. Port PDF generation utilities.
7. Wire up the Cloudinary signed-upload flow and the `getDocumentUrl` normalizer everywhere documents/photos render.
8. Add PWA manifest + service worker.
9. Run `next build` with static export and smoke-test the output; fix anything incompatible with static export (no API routes, no dynamic server functions).
10. Write `MIGRATION_NOTES.md` documenting every assumption made where the original implementation details weren't fully specified (e.g. `vehicle_checklists` exact columns), and `README.md` with full setup/deploy instructions.

Confirm your understanding of this scope, then start with step 1.

## ROLE

You are a senior full-stack engineer. You are rebuilding an existing production fleet-management PWA (currently vanilla HTML/CSS/JS, no framework, no bundler) into a **Next.js application** with a clean, organized, scalable folder structure. This is a **1:1 functional rebuild** — every feature, table, form, role, permission, and workflow listed below must exist in the new app. Do not drop or "simplify away" any feature. If something is ambiguous, make a reasonable decision and note it in a `MIGRATION_NOTES.md` file rather than skipping it.

## HARD CONSTRAINTS

1. **Framework**: Next.js 14+, App Router (`app/` directory).
2. **Static export**: The app MUST be able to build with `next export` / `output: 'export'` in `next.config.js` so it can be deployed as a static site. Do **not** use Next.js Server Actions, API routes (`app/api/*`), Middleware, or any server-only runtime feature that breaks static export — all backend logic must live in **Supabase** (Postgres + RLS + Auth + Edge Functions), called directly from client components, exactly like the original app does. Treat Next.js purely as a structured frontend build tool replacing the hand-written HTML/JS, not as a backend.

**Context & Goal:** I want to clean up my repository to reduce its size, remove clutter, and improve maintainability—**without breaking any existing functionality**. I need a detailed, surgical audit of my files.

**Category A: [SAFE TO DELETE] - 100% Redundant (No Functional Impact)**
- Compiled Python bytecode (`__pycache__/`, `*.pyc`, `*.pyo`).
- System junk files (`.DS_Store`, `Thumbs.db`, `*.tmp`, `*.log`).
- Dependency lockfiles that are no longer standard (e.g., `yarn.lock` if using `npm`, or vice versa).
- Duplicate backup files (e.g., `file~`, `file.bak`).

**Category B: [SAFE TO IGNORE] - Files to add to .gitignore (not delete from local, just stop tracking)**
- Local environment configs (`.env.local`, `.env.development`).
- Editor-specific folders (`.vscode/`, `.idea/`).
- Build caches (`.vite/`, `.next/`, `.nuxt/`, `.parcel-cache/`).
- Package manager install folders (`node_modules/`, `venv/`, `vendor/`).
- Test coverage folders (`coverage/`, `.nyc_output`).

**Category C: [REQUIRES VERIFICATION] - Dead Code & Unused Assets**
- Analyze `package.json` / `requirements.txt` - identify **unused dependencies** by checking if they are imported anywhere in the source code.

- Identify JavaScript/Typescript files that are never imported or required in the entry points.
- *Action:* Suggest these for deletion but require manual confirmation.

**Category D: [DO NOT DELETE] - Critical Infrastructure**
- Explicitly flag `.git`, `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml`, `README.md`, `LICENSE`, `.github/` workflows, and core configuration files (e.g., `vite.config.js`, `webpack.config.js`, `next.config.js`) as **untouchable** unless explicitly confirmed by the user.

**Step 3: Generate a "Surgical Cleanup Report":**
Structure your output exactly as follows:

1. **Executive Summary:** Total files, total size, and estimated size savings.
2. **Recommended `.gitignore` Update:** Provide the exact lines to add to my `.gitignore`.
3. **Deletion Checklist (Grouped by Safety):**
   - **Group 1 (Run immediately):** List files/folders to delete via terminal commands.
   - **Group 2 (Verify & Delete):** List unused dependencies with the command to uninstall them.
   - **Group 3 (Review manually):** List potentially unused source-code files with a note on why they seem redundant.
4. **Post-Cleanup Validation Checklist:** A list of commands I should run *after* deleting to ensure the build/test/pipeline still passes (e.g., `npm run build`, `pytest`, `cargo check`).

**Final Instruction:** Before I execute anything, I want you to write a small bash/PowerShell script that performs *only* the **Group 1 (Run immediately)** deletions, so I can review the script before running it. Do not automatically run destructive commands.
Or Generate me a prompt I can feed into codex/replit to perform the changes for me and also explain why and what get removed

input.file_text: # Task: Add Regional Data Separation (Cape Town / Joburg) to the INYATHI Fleet PWA ## Context This is a Supabase + vanilla JS PWA (no build step). Key files: - `schema.sql` — master schema (run once on fresh installs) - `supabase/migrations/*.sql` — incremental migrations (numbered, idempotent) - `config.js` — shared frontend config object `CONFIG` - `app.js` — shared Supabase client (`sb`), auth (`initAuth`), helpers - `admin.js` + `index.html` — admin dashboard (Calendar, Fleet, Drivers, etc. tabs) - `driver-dashboard.js` / `driver-dashboard.html` — driver-facing app (no changes needed here) - `supabase/functions/driver-invite/index.ts` — edge function that invites a new driver and creates their `profiles` row Two tables matter here: - `public.profiles` (drivers; `role = 'driver'`) - `public.bookings` Goal: introduce a `location` field on both tables (`'Cape Town'` or `'Joburg'`), add an admin-only region toggle that scopes every booking/driver query to the selected region, and make sure new bookings and newly invited drivers are automatically tagged with the region that was active when they were created. --- ## 1. Database changes Create a new migration file: `supabase/migrations/20260621000000_add_region_location.sql` Requirements: - Add `location TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Cape Town' CHECK (location IN ('Cape Town','Joburg'))` to `public.profiles`. - Add `location TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Cape Town' CHECK (location IN ('Cape Town','Joburg'))` to `public.bookings`. - Use `ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS` for idempotency, matching the style of existing migrations in this repo. - Add indexes: `idx_profiles_location` and `idx_bookings_location`. - Do **not** add `location` to `vehicles`, `rented_vehicles`, `inspections`, `recon_sheets`, etc. — fleet vehicles remain shared across regions unless I ask otherwise later. - Backfill existing rows to `'Cape Town'` via the column default (no separate UPDATE needed since `NOT NULL DEFAULT` handles it on `ADD COLUMN`). - Update `public.handle_new_user()` (the trigger that auto-creates a profile row on signup) so it still works — it does not need to set `location` itself; that will be done by the `driver-invite` edge function after invite (see Section 3). Just make sure the new `NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Cape Town'` column doesn't break the trigger's `INSERT`. - Mirror these two `ALTER TABLE` blocks into `schema.sql` as well (near where `profiles` and `bookings` are originally defined, or in a clearly marked "REGION SUPPORT" section near the bottom with the other additive blocks), so fresh installs get the column without needing the migration. --- ## 2. Shared config In `config.js`, add a single source of truth for valid regions so the toggle UI and any validation use the same list: ```js LOCATIONS: ['Cape Town', 'Joburg'], ``` --- ## 3. Driver invite flow — auto-tag new drivers with the active region `supabase/functions/driver-invite/index.ts` currently accepts `{ email, fullName }` in the POST body and upserts a `driver_invites` row, then calls `adminClient.auth.admin.inviteUserByEmail`. Changes: - Accept an additional `location` field in the request body. Validate it's one of `'Cape Town' | 'Joburg'`; reject with 400 if missing/invalid. - Store `location` on the `driver_invites` upsert (add a `location` column to `driver_invites` too, in the same migration as Section 1 — `ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS location TEXT`). - After the user accepts the invite and `handle_new_user()` creates their `profiles` row (default `'Cape Town'`), there's no direct way for the edge function to set it at invite time since the profile doesn't exist yet. Instead: have `driver-signup.html`'s post-signup flow (where it currently does `sb.from('profiles').update({ role:'driver', is_active:true })`) also set `location` by reading it from the matching `driver_invites` row (`select location from driver_invites where email = ...`) and including it in that same update call. In `admin.js`: - `inviteDriver(email, fullName)` → change signature to `inviteDriver(email, fullName, location)` and include `location` in the `sb.functions.invoke('driver-invite', { body: { email, fullName, location } })` call. - In the `form-driver` submit handler (the block calling `inviteDriver`), pass the currently active toggle region (see Section 4) as the `location` argument when creating a **new** driver (`!id` branch). When **editing** an existing driver, do not change their location automatically — but optionally add a read-only "Region" field to the edit view of `modal-driver` showing `driver-active-group`'s sibling, sourced from `profiles.location`, with an admin-editable `

This is the mechanism that already prevents double-booking; it must not become region-aware. --- ## 2. Shared config In `config.js`, add a single source of truth for valid regions so the toggle UI uses one list: ```js LOCATIONS: ['Cape Town', 'Joburg'], ``` --- ## 3. Admin region toggle (frontend) ### 3.1 UI In `index.html`, inside `.header-actions` (next to `.header-search`), add a small segmented toggle: ```html
``` Add matching styles in `style.css` (small pill buttons, active state using `var(--amber)`/`var(--navy)`, consistent with the existing `.badge`/`.btn-sm` look). ### 3.2 State In `admin.js`, near the top-level state declarations (alongside `calDate`, `allBookings`): ```js const REGION_STORAGE_KEY = 'inyathi-admin-region'; btn.addEventListener('click', () => setRegion(btn.dataset.region)); }); } function setRegion(region) { if (region === currentRegion) return; currentRegion = region; localStorage.setItem(REGION_STORAGE_KEY, region); document.querySelectorAll('.region-toggle-btn').forEach((btn) => btn.classList.toggle('active', btn.dataset.region === region) ); refreshRegionScopedData(); } async function refreshRegionScopedData() { await loadPendingDeletionsBadge(); const activeTab = document.querySelector('.tab-btn.active')?.dataset.tab || 'calendar'; switchTab(activeTab); } ``` Note: `loadBookingDropdowns()` (drivers/vehicles for the booking form) is **not** called here — those lists are shared across regions and don't change when the toggle changes. ### 3.3 Add `.eq('location', currentRegion)` to *display* queries only Add the region filter to these `bookings` queries in `admin.js`: - `renderCalendar()` — the `bookings` select that drives the month grid - `loadCalendarStats()` — the stats `bookings` select - `loadBookingsArchive()` — the archive table query - `loadActiveTrips()` / `loadUpcomingTrips()` (Drivers tab "Active/Upcoming Trips") - `loadPendingDeletionsDetail()` — join through `bookings` so deletion requests shown only cover the active region's bookings (filter on the joined `bookings.location`); `loadPendingDeletionsBadge()`'s count should match - Traffic Fines dashboard (`loadAdminTrafficFines`) — join via `bookings!traffic_fines_booking_id_fkey(location, invoice_no, client_name)` and filter on it ### 3.4 Do NOT add region filtering to: - `validateVehicleAvailability()` and `validateDriverAvailability()` — these must keep checking overlaps against **all** bookings regardless of region, exactly as they do today. This is the most important constraint in this task — do not let the toggle leak into these two functions. - `loadFleet()`, `loadBookingDropdowns()` (vehicle and driver `` dropdowns inside the booking modal show the full shared pool regardless of which region is toggled. 8. Editing an existing booking does not change its `location`. Please implement this end-to-end (migration + `schema.sql` update + `config.js` + `admin.js` + `index.html`/`style.css`), and explicitly call out in your summary that you verified item 6 above (the cross-region overlap check) still works, since that's the part most likely to regress if scoping is applied too broadly.

Updated with the key changes:

- **`vehicles` now gets a `location` column too** (its current home base), alongside `profiles` and `bookings`.
- **Hard validation, not just filtering**: vehicle/driver dropdowns on the booking form are pre-filtered to the booking's region *and* labeled with their location, but `validateVehicleAvailability`/`validateDriverAvailability` also get a location-match check as a backstop — so a mismatched assignment is rejected with a specific error even if the dropdown state goes stale.
- **Editing a booking re-scopes the dropdowns to that booking's own region**, not the header toggle's current value — so an admin can still edit a Joburg booking correctly while the toggle happens to be on Cape Town.
- **Independent local filters** on the Fleet tab and Manage Drivers table (Location + Active/Inactive), separate from the global header toggle — so admins can browse the full fleet/driver list across both regions when planning, then narrow down.
- **Rented vehicles are explicitly excluded** from location scoping, since they're sourced ad hoc per booking rather than from the shared fleet.

One judgment call baked into the prompt that you should sanity-check: I told the agent to treat vehicle/driver **relocation** as an explicit admin action only (via the vehicle/driver edit modal), never automatic — e.g. assigning a Cape Town vehicle to a Joburg booking is simply blocked, it doesn't auto-move the vehicle to Joburg. If you actually want assignment to *relocate* the vehicle/driver instead of blocking, that's a meaningfully different design and I can rewrite that section.

const { google } = require('googleapis');

function getAuth() {

content.text:
1	---
     2	name: frontend-design
     3	description: Guidance for distinctive, intentional visual design when building new UI or reshaping an existing one. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that don't read as templated defaults.
     4	license: Complete terms in LICENSE.txt
     5	---
     6	
     7	# Frontend Design
     8	
     9	Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for giving every client a visual identity that could not be mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take one real aesthetic risk you can justify.
    10	
    11	## Ground it in the subject
    12	
    13	If the brief does not pin down what the product or subject is, pin it yourself before designing: name one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job, and state your choice. If there's any information in your memory about the human's preferences, context about what they're building, or designs you've made before – use that as a hint. The subject's own world, its materials, instruments, artifacts, and vernacular, is where distinctive choices come from. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.
    14	
    15	## Design principles
    16	
    17	For web designs, the hero is a thesis. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in whatever form makes sense for it: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the template answer, only use if that's truly the best option.
    18	
    19	Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.
    20	
    21	Structure is information. Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.
    22	
    23	Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated.
    24	
    25	Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
    26	
    27	Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.
    28	
    29	## Process: brainstorm, explore, plan, critique, build, critique again
    30	
    31	For calibration: AI-generated design right now clusters around three looks: (1) a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta accent; (2) a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent; (3) a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns. All three are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. Just like a human designer who's hired, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.
    32	
    33	Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the human's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and signature. Color: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values. Type: the typefaces for 2+ roles (a characterful display face that's used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed). Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Signature: the single unique element this page will be remembered by that embodies the brief in an appropriate way.
    34	
    35	Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan exactly and deriving every color and type decision from it.
    36	
    37	When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and a element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with paddings/margins between sections.
    38	
    39	Try to do a lot of this planning and iteration in your thinking, and only show ideas to the user when you have higher confidence it'll delight them.
    40	
    41	## Restraint and self-critique
    42	
    43	Spend your boldness in one place. Let the signature element be the one memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Not taking a risk can be a risk itself! Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots if your environment supports it – a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creators have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.
    44	
    45	## More on writing in design
    46	
    47	Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand, and therefore easier to use. They are design material, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality to copy that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.
    48	
    49	Write from the end user's side of the screen. Name things by what people control and recognize, never by how the system is built. A person manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific is always better than being clever.
    50	
    51	Use active voice as default. A control should say exactly what happens when it's used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.
    52	
    53	Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.
    54	
    55	Keep the register conversational and tuned: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each element do exactly one job. A label labels, an example demonstrates, and nothing quietly does double duty.
    56

Here are four different visual approaches to displaying booking spans on a calendar, from simplest to most informative. After the mockups, I'll explain the tradeoffs.
```
This block is not supported on your current device yet.
```

Here's a breakdown of each approach and my recommendation for your specific codebase:

**Option 1 — thin stripes** is the best drop-in improvement for what you already have. Your current code already builds `calendarMap` per day and renders dots in a `booking-markers` div — you'd just change each `span.booking-marker` from a circle to a short wide rectangle (e.g. `border-radius: 2px`, `width: 100%`, `height: 5px`). It takes about 5 lines of CSS. Overlapping bookings stack vertically as multiple stripes, which is natural and readable.

**Option 2 — pill spans** (Google Calendar style) is the most powerful but also the hardest to build. The challenge is that your calendar renders day-by-day, so you'd need to track which bookings started before the current row and continue rendering a "mid" pill with no label. It also breaks at week boundaries (Saturday → Sunday). Doable, but it requires restructuring your `renderCalendar` loop to think in rows, not individual days.

**Option 3 — left border + badge** is the easiest to implement of all four. Just add `border-left: 3px solid {vehicleColor}` on the `.cal-day` element for active bookings, and drop a tiny truncated label inside on the first day of a booking. Zero change to your `booking-markers` logic — you'd just apply a `style` attribute directly to each `.cal-day` div.

**My recommendation for your codebase:** go with Option 1. The change is minimal — in your `renderCalendar()` function in `admin.js`, replace the dot `<span>` with a stripe `<div>`, and update your `.booking-marker` CSS from a circle to a rectangle. You keep all the existing tooltip, color mapping, and click logic exactly as-is.

content.text:
# Imagine — Visual Creation Suite ## Modules Call read_me again with the modules parameter to load detailed guidance: - `diagram` — SVG flowcharts, structural diagrams, illustrative diagrams - `mockup` — UI mockups, forms, cards, dashboards - `interactive` — interactive explainers with controls - `chart` — charts, data analysis, geographic maps (Chart.js, D3 choropleth) - `art` — illustration and generative art Pick the closest fit. The module includes all relevant design guidance. **Complexity budget — hard limits:** - Box subtitles: ≤5 words. Detail goes in click-through (`sendPrompt`) or the prose below — not the box. - Colors: ≤2 ramps per diagram. If colors encode meaning (states, tiers), add a 1-line legend. Otherwise use one neutral ramp. - Horizontal tier: ≤4 boxes at full width (~140px each). 5+ boxes → shrink to ≤110px OR wrap to 2 rows OR split into overview + detail diagrams. If you catch yourself writing "click to learn more" in prose, the diagram itself must ACTUALLY be sparse. Don't promise brevity then front-load everything. **Accessibility:** For HTML widgets, begin with a visually-hidden `

` containing a one-sentence summary of the visualization for screen-reader users. (SVG widgets use `role="img"` with `` and `<desc>` instead — see SVG setup.) You create rich visual content — SVG diagrams/illustrations and HTML interactive widgets — that renders inline in conversation. The best output feels like a natural extension of the chat. ## Core Design System These rules apply to ALL use cases. ### Philosophy - **Seamless**: Users shouldn't notice where claude.ai ends and your widget begins. - **Flat**: No gradients, mesh backgrounds, noise textures, or decorative effects. Clean flat surfaces. - **Compact**: Show the essential inline. Explain the rest in text. - **Text goes in your response, visuals go in the tool** — All explanatory text, descriptions, introductions, and summaries must be written as normal response text OUTSIDE the tool call. The tool output should contain ONLY the visual element (diagram, chart, interactive widget). Never put paragraphs of explanation, section headings, or descriptive prose inside the HTML/SVG. If the user asks "explain X", write the explanation in your response and use the tool only for the visual that accompanies it. The user's font settings only apply to your response text, not to text inside the widget. ### Streaming Output streams token-by-token. Structure code so useful content appears early. - **HTML**: `<style>` (short) → content HTML → `<script>` last. - **SVG**: `<defs>` (markers) → visual elements immediately. - Prefer inline `style="..."` over `<style>` blocks — inputs/controls must look correct mid-stream. - Keep `<style>` under ~15 lines. Interactive widgets with inputs and sliders need more style rules — that's fine, but don't bloat with decorative CSS. - Gradients, shadows, and blur flash during streaming DOM diffs. Use solid flat fills instead. ### Rules - No `<!-- comments -->` or `/* comments */` (waste tokens, break streaming) - No font-size below 11px - No emoji. Icons = Tabler **outline** webfont (5800+, already loaded): `<i class="ti ti-home"></i>`. Outline only — never use `-filled` suffixes (`ti-heart-filled` etc. are not loaded and will render blank). Inherits color + font-size from parent. Decorative icons get `aria-hidden="true"`; icon-only buttons get `aria-label`. Common: ti-home ti-settings ti-user ti-search ti-x ti-check ti-plus ti-trash ti-edit ti-download ti-upload ti-file ti-folder ti-chart-bar ti-calendar ti-clock ti-arrow-right ti-arrow-left ti-chevron-down ti-external-link ti-copy ti-refresh ti-player-play ti-player-pause ti-heart ti-star ti-bell ti-mail ti-lock ti-eye ti-menu-2. Don't hand-draw icon SVG paths. - No gradients, drop shadows, blur, glow, or neon effects - No dark/colored backgrounds on outer containers (transparent only — host provides the bg) - **Typography**: The default font is Anthropic Sans. For the rare editorial/blockquote moment, use `font-family: var(--font-serif)`. - **Headings**: h1 = 22px, h2 = 18px, h3 = 16px — all `font-weight: 500`. Heading color is pre-set to `var(--color-text-primary)` — don't override it. Body text = 16px, weight 400, `line-height: 1.7`. **Two weights only: 400 regular, 500 bold.** Never use 600 or 700 — they look heavy against the host UI. - **Sentence case** always. Never Title Case, never ALL CAPS. This applies everywhere including SVG text labels and diagram headings. - **No mid-sentence bolding**, including in your response text around the tool call. Entity names, class names, function names go in `code style` not **bold**. Bold is for headings and labels only. - The widget container is `display: block; width: 100%`. Your HTML fills it naturally — no wrapper div needed. Just start with your content directly. If you want vertical breathing room, add `padding: 1rem 0` on your first element. - Never use `position: fixed` — the iframe viewport sizes itself to your in-flow content height, so fixed-positioned elements (modals, overlays, tooltips) collapse it to `min-height: 100px`. For modal/overlay mockups: wrap everything in a normal-flow `<div style="min-height: 400px; background: rgba(0,0,0,0.45); display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center;">` and put the modal inside — it's a faux viewport that actually contributes layout height. - No DOCTYPE, `<html>`, `<head>`, or `<body>` — just content fragments. - When placing text on a colored background (badges, pills, cards, tags), use the darkest shade from that same color family for the text — never plain black or generic gray. - **Corners**: use `border-radius: var(--border-radius-md)` (or `-lg` for cards) in HTML. In SVG, `rx="4"` is the default — larger values make pills, use only when you mean a pill. - **No rounded corners on single-sided borders** — if using `border-left` or `border-top` accents, set `border-radius: 0`. Rounded corners only work with full borders on all sides. - **No titles or prose inside the tool output** — see Philosophy above. - **Icon sizing**: Tabler `<i class="ti …">` sizes with `font-size` — 16–20px inline, 24px max decorative. For one-off inline SVG icons, set `width`/`height` explicitly (same limits). - No tabs, carousels, or `display: none` sections during streaming — hidden content streams invisibly. Show all content stacked vertically. (Post-streaming JS-driven steppers are fine — see Illustrative/Interactive sections.) - No nested scrolling — auto-fit height. - Scripts execute after streaming — load libraries via `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` (UMD globals), then use the global in a plain `<script>` that follows. - **CDN allowlist (CSP-enforced)**: external resources may ONLY load from `cdnjs.cloudflare.com`, `esm.sh`, `cdn.jsdelivr.net`, `unpkg.com`, `fonts.googleapis.com`, `fonts.gstatic.com`. All other origins are blocked by the sandbox — the request silently fails. ### CSS Variables **Backgrounds**: `--color-background-primary` (white), `-secondary` (surfaces), `-tertiary` (page bg), `-info`, `-danger`, `-success`, `-warning` **Text**: `--color-text-primary` (black), `-secondary` (muted), `-tertiary` (hints), `-info`, `-danger`, `-success`, `-warning` **Borders**: `--color-border-tertiary` (0.15α, default), `-secondary` (0.3α, hover), `-primary` (0.4α), semantic `-info/-danger/-success/-warning` **Typography**: `--font-sans`, `--font-serif`, `--font-mono` **Layout**: `--border-radius-md` (8px), `--border-radius-lg` (12px — preferred for most components), `--border-radius-xl` (16px) All auto-adapt to light/dark mode. For custom colors in HTML, use CSS variables. **Dark mode is mandatory** — every color must work in both modes: - In SVG: use the pre-built color classes (`c-blue`, `c-teal`, `c-amber`, etc.) for colored nodes — they handle light/dark mode automatically. Never write `<style>` blocks for colors. - In SVG: every `<text>` element needs a class (`t`, `ts`, `th`) — never omit fill or use `fill="inherit"`. Inside a `c-{color}` parent, text classes auto-adjust to the ramp. - In HTML: always use CSS variables (--color-text-primary, --color-text-secondary) for text. Never hardcode colors like color: #333 — invisible in dark mode. - Mental test: if the background were near-black, would every text element still be readable? ### sendPrompt(text) A global function that sends a message to chat as if the user typed it. Use it when the user's next step benefits from Claude thinking. Handle filtering, sorting, toggling, and calculations in JS instead. ### Links `<a href="https://...">` just works — clicks are intercepted and open the host's link-confirmation dialog. Or call `openLink(url)` directly. ## When nothing fits Pick the closest use case below and adapt. When nothing fits cleanly: - Default to editorial layout if the content is explanatory - Default to card layout if the content is a bounded object - All core design system rules still apply - Use `sendPrompt()` for any action that benefits from Claude thinking ## UI components ### Layout width The widget container is 380px wide. **Mobile column cap.** The widget container is ~380px wide — never lay out more than TWO columns of cards, stats, controls, or option grids. Three-up at this width is unreadable: card content wraps to 3-4 lines and tap targets fall below 44px. Use `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(160px, 1fr))` (which naturally tops out at 2 here) or `repeat(2, minmax(0, 1fr))` explicitly. If you have 3+ items, stack them in 2-col rows or go single-column; do not write `repeat(3, …)` or `repeat(4, …)`. ### Aesthetic Flat, clean, white surfaces. Minimal 0.5px borders. Generous whitespace. No gradients, no shadows (except functional focus rings). Everything should feel native to claude.ai — like it belongs on the page, not embedded from somewhere else. ### Tokens - Borders: always `0.5px solid var(--color-border-tertiary)` (or `-secondary` for emphasis) - Corner radius: `var(--border-radius-md)` for most elements, `var(--border-radius-lg)` for cards - Cards: white bg (`var(--color-background-primary)`), 0.5px border, radius-lg, padding 1rem 1.25rem - Form elements (input, select, textarea, button, range slider) are pre-styled — write bare tags. Text inputs are 36px with hover/focus built in; range sliders have 4px track + 18px thumb; buttons have outline style with hover/active. Only add inline styles to override (e.g., different width). - Buttons: pre-styled with transparent bg, 0.5px border-secondary, hover bg-secondary, active scale(0.98). If it triggers sendPrompt, append a ↗ arrow. - **Round every displayed number.** JS float math leaks artifacts — `0.1 + 0.2` gives `0.30000000000000004`, `7 * 1.1` gives `7.700000000000001`. Any number that reaches the screen (slider readouts, stat card values, axis labels, data-point labels, tooltips, computed totals) must go through `Math.round()`, `.toFixed(n)`, or `Intl.NumberFormat`. Pick the precision that makes sense for the context — integers for counts, 1–2 decimals for percentages, `toLocaleString()` for currency. For range sliders, also set `step="1"` (or step="0.1" etc.) so the input itself emits round values. - Spacing: use rem for vertical rhythm (1rem, 1.5rem, 2rem), px for component-internal gaps (8px, 12px, 16px) - Box-shadows: none, except `box-shadow: 0 0 0 Npx` focus rings on inputs ### Metric cards For summary numbers (revenue, count, percentage) — surface card with muted 13px label above, 24px/500 number below. `background: var(--color-background-secondary)`, no border, `border-radius: var(--border-radius-md)`, padding 1rem. Use in grids of 2-4 with `gap: 12px`. Distinct from raised cards (which have white bg + border). ### Layout - Editorial (explanatory content): no card wrapper, prose flows naturally - Card (bounded objects like a contact record, receipt): single raised card wraps the whole thing - Don't put tables here — output them as markdown in your response text **Grid overflow:** `grid-template-columns: 1fr` has `min-width: auto` by default — children with large min-content push the column past the container. Use `minmax(0, 1fr)` to clamp. **Table overflow:** Tables with many columns auto-expand past `width: 100%` if cell contents exceed it. In constrained layouts (≤700px), use `table-layout: fixed` and set explicit column widths, or reduce columns, or allow horizontal scroll on a wrapper. ### Mockup presentation Contained mockups — mobile screens, chat threads, single cards, modals, small UI components — should sit on a background surface (`var(--color-background-secondary)` container with `border-radius: var(--border-radius-lg)` and padding, or a device frame) so they don't float naked on the widget canvas. Full-width mockups like dashboards, settings pages, or data tables that naturally fill the viewport do not need an extra wrapper. ### 1. Interactive explainer — learn how something works *"Explain how compound interest works" / "Teach me about sorting algorithms"* Use HTML for the interactive controls — sliders, buttons, live state displays, charts. Keep prose explanations in your normal response text (outside the tool call), not embedded in the HTML. No card wrapper. Whitespace is the container. ```html <div style="display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 12px; margin: 0 0 1.5rem;"> <label style="font-size: 14px; color: var(--color-text-secondary);">Years</label> <input type="range" min="1" max="40" value="20" id="years" style="flex: 1;" /> <span style="font-size: 14px; font-weight: 500; min-width: 24px;" id="years-out">20</span> </div> <div style="display: flex; align-items: baseline; gap: 8px; margin: 0 0 1.5rem;"> <span style="font-size: 14px; color: var(--color-text-secondary);">£1,000 →</span> <span style="font-size: 24px; font-weight: 500;" id="result">£3,870</span> </div> <div style="margin: 2rem 0; position: relative; height: 240px;"> <canvas id="chart"></canvas> </div> ``` Use `sendPrompt()` to let users ask follow-ups: `sendPrompt('What if I increase the rate to 10%?')` ### 2. Compare options — decision making *"Compare pricing and features of these products" / "Help me choose between React and Vue"* Use HTML. Side-by-side card grid for options. Highlight differences with semantic colors. Interactive elements for filtering or weighting. - Each option in a card. Use badges for key differentiators. A leading Tabler icon (`<i class="ti ti-NAME">` at 20px, `aria-hidden`) anchors each option visually — pick the most apt name per option. - Add `sendPrompt()` buttons: `sendPrompt('Tell me more about the Pro plan')` - Don't put comparison tables inside this tool — output them as regular markdown tables in your response text instead. The tool is for the visual card grid only. - When one option is recommended or "most popular", accent its card with `border: 2px solid var(--color-border-info)` only (2px is deliberate — the only exception to the 0.5px rule, used to accent featured items) — keep the same background and border as the other cards. Add a small badge (e.g. "Most popular") above or inside the card header using `background: var(--color-background-info); color: var(--color-text-info); font-size: 12px; padding: 4px 12px; border-radius: var(--border-radius-md)`. ### 3. Data record — bounded UI object *"Show me a Salesforce contact card" / "Create a receipt for this order"* Use HTML. Wrap the entire thing in a single raised card. All content is sans-serif since it's pure UI. Use an avatar/initials circle for people (see example below). ```html <div style="background: var(--color-background-primary); border-radius: var(--border-radius-lg); border: 0.5px solid var(--color-border-tertiary); padding: 1rem 1.25rem;"> <div style="display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 12px; margin-bottom: 16px;"> <div style="width: 44px; height: 44px; border-radius: 50%; background: var(--color-background-info); display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; font-weight: 500; font-size: 14px; color: var(--color-text-info);">MR</div> <div> <p style="font-weight: 500; font-size: 15px; margin: 0;">Maya Rodriguez</p> <p style="font-size: 13px; color: var(--color-text-secondary); margin: 0;">VP of Engineering</p> </div> </div> <div style="border-top: 0.5px solid var(--color-border-tertiary); padding-top: 12px;"> <table style="width: 100%; font-size: 13px;"> <tr><td style="color: var(--color-text-secondary); Don't cycle through colors like a rainbow (step 1 = blue, step 2 = amber, step 3 = red...). Instead: - Group nodes by **category** — all nodes of the same type share one color. E.g. in a vaccine diagram: all immune cells = purple, all pathogens = coral, all outcomes = teal. - For illustrative diagrams, map colors to **physical properties** — warm ramps for heat/energy, cool for cold/calm, green for organic, gray for structural/inert. - Use **gray for neutral/structural** nodes (start, end, generic steps). - Use **2-3 colors per diagram**, not 6+. More colors = more visual noise. A diagram with gray + purple + teal is cleaner than one using every ramp. - **Prefer purple, teal, coral, pink** for general diagram categories. Reserve blue, green, amber, and red for cases where the node genuinely represents an informational, success, warning, or error concept — those colors carry strong semantic connotations from UI conventions. (Exception: illustrative diagrams may use blue/amber/red freely when they map to physical properties like temperature or pressure.) **Text on colored backgrounds:** Always use the 800 or 900 stop from the same ramp as the fill. Never use black, gray, or --color-text-primary on colored fills. **When a box has both a title and a subtitle, they must be two different stops** — title darker (800 in light mode, 100 in dark), subtitle lighter (600 in light, 200 in dark). Same stop for both reads flat; the weight difference alone isn't enough. For example, text on Blue 50 (#E6F1FB) must use Blue 800 (#0C447C) or 900 (#042C53), not black. This applies to SVG text elements inside colored rects, and to HTML badges, pills, and labels with colored backgrounds. **Light/dark mode quick pick** — use only stops from the table, never off-table hex values: - **Light mode**: 50 fill + 600 stroke + **800 title / 600 subtitle** - **Dark mode**: 800 fill + 200 stroke + **100 title / 200 subtitle** - Apply `c-{ramp}` to a `<g>` wrapping shape+text, or directly to a `<rect>`/`<circle>`/`<ellipse>`. Never to `<path>` — paths don't get ramp fill. For colored connector strokes use inline `stroke="#..."` (any mid-ramp hex works in both modes). Dark mode is automatic for ramp classes. Available: c-gray, c-blue, c-red, c-amber, c-green, c-teal, c-purple, c-coral, c-pink. For status/semantic meaning in UI (success, warning, danger) use CSS variables. For categorical coloring in both diagrams and UI, use these ramps.

Here's a breakdown of each approach and my recommendation for your specific codebase:

**Option 1 — thin stripes** is the best drop-in improvement for what you already have. Your current code already builds `calendarMap` per day and renders dots in a `booking-markers` div — you'd just change each `span.booking-marker` from a circle to a short wide rectangle (e.g. `border-radius: 2px`, `width: 100%`, `height: 5px`). It takes about 5 lines of CSS. Overlapping bookings stack vertically as multiple stripes, which is natural and readable.

**Option 2 — pill spans** (Google Calendar style) is the most powerful but also the hardest to build. The challenge is that your calendar renders day-by-day, so you'd need to track which bookings started before the current row and continue rendering a "mid" pill with no label. It also breaks at week boundaries (Saturday → Sunday). Doable, but it requires restructuring your `renderCalendar` loop to think in rows, not individual days.

**Option 3 — left border + badge** is the easiest to implement of all four. Just add `border-left: 3px solid {vehicleColor}` on the `.cal-day` element for active bookings, and drop a tiny truncated label inside on the first day of a booking. Zero change to your `booking-markers` logic — you'd just apply a `style` attribute directly to each `.cal-day` div.

**My recommendation for your codebase:** go with Option 1. The change is minimal — in your `renderCalendar()` function in `admin.js`, replace the dot `<span>` with a stripe `<div>`, and update your `.booking-marker` CSS from a circle to a rectangle. You keep all the existing tooltip, color mapping, and click logic exactly as-is.

Here's the thinking behind each one for your specific situation:

Option A (heat map) works best when you care about capacity pressure — "are we overloaded this week?" — rather than individual vehicle tracking. Implementation is dead simple: count bookings per day, map the count to a blue intensity stop, apply it as a background colour on the `.cal-day` element. No structure change needed.

Option B (swimlane) is the most powerful for fleet management specifically. Instead of asking "what's happening on day X?", it answers "is vehicle Y available?" — which is arguably more useful when you're dispatching. This would live as a separate "Fleet View" tab in your admin sidebar rather than replacing the calendar.

Option C (Gantt timeline) is already essentially what your Bookings Archive table does, but rendered visually. You could add it as a toggle below your existing calendar — same data, different rendering. The hard part is computing left-offset percentages from your `start_date`/`end_date` relative to the visible window.

Option D (weekly grid) is purpose-built for the dispatching question: "I need a vehicle for Thursday, which ones are free?" It only works well up to about 6–7 vehicles before it gets too wide for mobile, but for a fleet that size it's excellent.

Option E (split panel) is actually the closest to what you already have — your day-click panel below the calendar is already doing the detail side. The main change would be making the calendar itself smaller and more compact (a "mini calendar" style), and making the right panel richer with proper booking cards instead of a flat list. On desktop this is a natural two-column layout; on mobile it would stack.

For your codebase, Option E with Option B as a separate fleet tab is probably the strongest combination — keep the calendar for date navigation, add a swimlane view for availability checking.
